definition: RAG — retrieval-augmented generation — means the AI searches your documents first, then writes its answer using what it found. Instead of relying on what it memorized during training, it works open-book: retrieve the relevant pages, then generate the answer from them.

edges.label: searches by meaning
edges.note: Retrieval ranks documents by embedding similarity, not keyword overlap.

edges.label: feeds pages into
edges.note: Retrieved chunks are pasted into the context window ahead of your question.

edges.label: cuts down on
edges.note: Answers grounded in your documents hallucinate far less.

example.body: You ask your company's assistant 'how many sick days do I get?' It searches the employee handbook, finds the leave section, hands those pages to the model along with your question, and the model answers 'six days' — quoting the handbook. Without retrieval it would have guessed from its training data and probably been wrong.
example.title: Asking about the vacation policy

footnotes.body: A production RAG pipeline: chunk documents into passages, embed each chunk, store vectors in a vector database, embed the query, retrieve top-k chunks by cosine similarity, concatenate them into the prompt, generate. Quality lives or dies on chunking and retrieval — garbage in, grounded-out.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

name: RAG
tagline: Letting the AI look things up before it answers — open-book instead of closed-book.
whyItMatters: RAG is the main practical answer to two big problems: hallucinations and stale knowledge. A model trained last year can't know your new HR policy — but with RAG it doesn't need to; it reads the policy first. Most serious AI products you use have some form of retrieval working under the hood.
